extra.message: Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on untrusted data (RCE) — Remote code execution on the Django server — attacker can read/write files, exfiltrate PII, pivot to internal network, or drop ransomware. [verified: Same as finding 1: user-supplied bytes optionally base64-decoded then deserialized via pickle.loads() with no integrity check, enabling arbitrary Python code execution.]

Code injection via eval() on user-controlled expression (RCE) — Remote code execution on the Django server — ability to read all employee records, compensation data, documents, and pivot to database/network. [verified: Same as finding 0: user-controlled 'expr' GET parameter passed to eval() with restricted builtins escapable via well-known Python sandbox bypass techniques.]

Remote code execution via pickle.loads on attacker-controlled data — Full remote code execution — attacker gains complete control of the Python process and can access all application data and secrets. [verified: Same as finding 1: user-supplied body/blob parameter passes through optional base64 decode directly to pickle.loads() enabling arbitrary code execution via malicious __reduce__ payloads.]

Code injection via eval() on user-supplied expression — Remote code execution — restricted eval can be escaped via introspection to access real Python builtins and execute arbitrary code. [verified: Same as finding 0: user-controlled 'expr' flows directly into eval() with restricted builtins that can be escaped via Python introspection chains to achieve arbitrary code execution.]

OS command injection via user-controlled host parameter in ping command — Remote code execution on the server — complete system compromise including access to employee PII, compensation data, and all files on disk. [verified: Same as finding 2: user-controlled 'host' parameter flows unsanitized into os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host); shell metacharacters enable arbitrary command execution with no escaping or validation.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 user-controlled fragment — Attacker executes arbitrary Python code on server; response rendered as text/html also enables reflected XSS. [verified: User-controlled 'fragment' GET parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered as text/html; SSTI enables arbitrary Python code execution via payloads like {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 — Remote code execution — Jinja2 SSTI allows reading server files, executing system commands, and accessing Python internals. The text/html content type also enables reflected XSS for simpler payloads. [verified: Same as finding 5: user-controlled 'fragment' concatenated into Jinja2 Template string rendered as text/html enables SSTI and arbitrary Python code execution.]

Path traversal — arbitrary file write via user-controlled filename and body — Arbitrary file write leading to remote code execution (web shell in static directory), application tampering, or denial of service via disk exhaustion. [verified: Same as finding 8: user-controlled 'name' and request.body written to path under BASE_EXPORT_DIR with mkdir parents=True and no traversal sanitization, enabling web shell planting or code overwrite.]

OS command injection via unsanitized shell command construction — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the Django process. [verified: Same as finding 2: user-controlled 'host' concatenated directly into shell command string executed via os.system() with no sanitization or escaping.]

OS Command Injection via shell probe ops route — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the Django process. Attacker can read/write any files, exfiltrate the database, pivot to internal infrastructure. [verified: Same as finding 2: user-controlled 'host' parameter concatenated unsanitized into os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) with no shell escaping, enabling arbitrary OS command execution.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Attackers can perform unlimited brute-force password guessing, credential stuffing, and token brute-forcing without any throttling or account lockout. [verified: No rate limiting package (django-axes, django-ratelimit) is installed; no custom throttle middleware, decorator, or manual attempt counter exists in accounts/views.py; the login and password-reset endpoints at accounts/urls.py:8 are reachable by unauthenticated attackers with unlimited retries, and the 10-char minimum password does not prevent credential-stuffing or brute-force.]

Missing rate limiting on all authentication endpoints — Attackers can perform unlimited brute-force attacks against login credentials, password reset tokens, and API keys, potentially compromising user accounts and gaining unauthorized access. [verified: All authentication endpoints — login, password reset, invite acceptance, API key auth (portal_api/services.py:authenticate_api_key), and the ops token gate (hr_portal/payroll_operations.py:_wrk_gate) — lack any rate-limiting mechanism: zero matches for throttle/ratelimit/axes packages, and _wrk_gate is a bare string comparison with no cooldown, allowing unlimited brute-force against credentials, t]

Path traversal — arbitrary file read via user-controlled filename — Arbitrary file disclosure — attacker can read /etc/passwd, .env files, database configuration, source code, and any file the process has permission to read. [verified: Same as finding 7: user-controlled 'packet_ref' joined to BASE_EXPORT_DIR without sanitization, then read_text() allows reading arbitrary files via path traversal sequences.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via user-controlled URL in urllib.request.urlopen — Access to internal/cloud-metadata endpoints, database ports, internal admin panels, credential leakage, and network pivot. [verified: Same as finding 3: user-controlled 'url' passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() with no host/scheme validation enabling SSRF to internal services and metadata endpoints.]

CORS misconfiguration: wildcard origin reflection with credentials — Malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests and read responses, enabling data theft if sessions or cookies are in scope. [verified: Response sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the unvalidated request Origin header AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to 'true'; any malicious origin can make credentialed cross-origin requests and read responses, defeating the same-origin policy.]

NoSQL injection — user-controlled MongoDB query filter — Arbitrary MongoDB query execution, potential JavaScript code execution on the database server, data exfiltration, denial of service. [verified: Same as finding 4: user-supplied JSON body used directly as MongoDB query filter in find_one() enabling NoSQL operator injection without sanitization.]

XXE via XML parsing with external entity resolution enabled — Arbitrary file read, SSRF to internal services, and denial of service via entity expansion attacks. [verified: Same as finding 6: lxml XMLParser with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False parses user-supplied XML enabling XXE-based file read and SSRF.]

Mass Assignment: Payroll Specialist Can Set HR-Internal visible_to_employee Flag on Document Uploads — A payroll specialist can upload payslips or tax forms with visible_to_employee=False, hiding them from the owning employee and their manager. The employee would not see their own payslip and receives no notification. This allows a lower-privileged role to exercise an HR-admin-only capability (marking documents as HR-internal). [verified: DocumentUploadForm.Meta.fields includes visible_to_employee (forms.py:18), the @hr_or_payroll_required view checks category but never overrides this HR-internal flag for payroll specialists, and form.save(commit=False) at views.py:151 copies attacker-controlled POST data directly into the model — contrast with employee_document_upload which explicitly forces visible_to_employee=True.]

CSV formula injection in payroll and onboarding exports — When a user opens the exported CSV in Excel or similar spreadsheet software, malicious formulas embedded in data fields can execute, potentially exfiltrating data or running commands. [verified: Same data flow as finding 0: user-controlled strings (names, policy titles, department names) reach csv.writer in all three export functions (_export_payroll, _export_onboarding, _export_policy_acks) with no formula-character prefixing or validation anywhere in the pipeline.]

CSV Formula Injection via Employee Display Name in Exports — When HR admin or payroll specialist opens exported CSV in Excel/Google Sheets, injected spreadsheet formulas execute, exfiltrating salary data and employee PII from exported cells to attacker-controlled servers, or executing local commands on the victim's machine (in older Excel with DDE enabled). [verified: display_name (first_name + last_name from ProfileUpdateForm with no formula-character validation) flows unsanitized into csv.writer output at line ~267 in _export_payroll; no prefixing neutralization exists in the csv.writer calls, and no clean_first_name/clean_last_name validator is implemented in any form.]

CSV Formula Injection in payroll/onboarding/policy exports — Code execution on the victim's machine when they open the exported CSV file in a spreadsheet application that evaluates formulas, leading to arbitrary command execution or data exfiltration from the spreadsheet user's system. [verified: Same data flow as finding 0: employee display_name and task/policy titles written via csv.writer in all three export functions; no single-quote prefix or formula-character stripping is applied, and no form-level validation blocks formula characters.]

CSV formula injection in payroll/onboarding/policy exports — Command execution on the victim's machine when the exported CSV is opened in a spreadsheet application — malware delivery, credential harvesting, or lateral movement within the corporate network. [verified: Same data flow as finding 0: emp.user.display_name and other user-controlled text fields pass unsanitized through csv.writer at lines ~264-273; no formula-injection defense (prefixing, validation, or post-processing) exists in any of the three export functions.]

CSV Formula Injection in Onboarding Export — An HR admin can embed spreadsheet formulas in onboarding task titles that execute when a payroll specialist downloads and opens the exported CSV in Excel/LibreOffice, leading to command execution (Windows) or credential/data exfiltration. [verified: t.title from OnboardingTask is set via TaskCreateForm (onboarding/forms.py) which has no formula-character validation; it reaches csv.writer at line ~307 in _export_onboarding without prefixing. The HR-admin-to-payroll-specialist trust boundary is still exploitable since payroll specialists are not expected to scrutinize task titles for formulas.]

CSV Formula Injection via Policy Acknowledgement Export — Remote code execution on the spreadsheet user's machine when the exported CSV is opened in Excel, LibreOffice, or similar. An employee can inject a malicious formula into their display name, which executes when HR/payroll staff open the exported file. [verified: a.policy.code and a.policy.title are set via PolicyForm/PolicyEditForm (policies/forms.py) with no formula-character validation; emp.user.display_name likewise unsanitized. All flow into csv.writer at line ~338+ in _export_policy_acks without neutralization prefixing.]

Missing authentication gate on ops endpoint — Unauthenticated users can access an internal ops endpoint, violating the expected security boundary. [verified: payroll_identity_ping_336 is the only ops endpoint without _wrk_gate() check, making it accessible without the x-internal-token header; confirms a gap in the ops token gate security boundary.]

Hardcoded secrets in source code — Anyone with repository access (including via leak) obtains the hardcoded verifier values, weakening the identity check. [verified: Function payroll_identity_hint_363 contains hardcoded verifier pairs {'north': '4812', 'south': '5930'} in plaintext source code committed to version control; anyone with repository access obtains the verifier values.]

Account/Handle Enumeration via Distinct Error Responses — An attacker with the ops token can enumerate valid handles, then potentially brute-force verifier values for known handles to gain access. [verified: payroll_identity_hint_363 returns distinct HTTP status codes (404 for unknown handle vs 403 for bad verifier), allowing an attacker with the ops token to enumerate valid handles by observing response differences.]

Missing access control token gate on ops route — Breaks the ops token gate boundary. Any unauthenticated user can access this internal ops endpoint, potentially leaking information or being used as an open proxy if the route is later modified with sensitive functionality. [verified: Same as finding 14: payroll_identity_ping_336 omits _wrk_gate() check, the only ops route without the x-internal-token header requirement.]

Missing authentication — ops endpoint exposed without token gate — Unauthenticated access to an internal operations endpoint. While the current behavior is benign, it exposes an internal route that may process or reflect user input without any security boundary. [verified: Same as finding 14: payroll_identity_ping_336 lacks _wrk_gate() check unlike all 18 other ops routes, allowing unauthenticated access to an internal operations endpoint.]

Vertical Privilege Escalation via Insufficient Role Check on Task Review — A payroll specialist or employee-role user assigned as someone's manager can approve, reject, or waive onboarding tasks, bypassing the intended role-based restriction that only managers and HR admins may review tasks. [verified: `_can_act_on_task` for `review` checks only `task.assignee.manager_id == user.id` without verifying `user.role == 'manager'`, unlike `compensation/views.py:163` and `hr_requests/views.py:185` which require both. `@any_role_required` admits payroll_specialist/employee, and CSV import (`employees/views_import_export.py:171-173`) sets manager with no role validation.]

Weak Token Gate — Non-Constant-Time Comparison for Ops Auth — A timing side-channel could allow an attacker to brute-force the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN value, gaining access to all 19 ops routes and their associated critical vulnerabilities (RCE, SSRF, SSTI, etc.). [verified: _wrk_gate uses simple string equality (==) for token comparison rather than constant-time comparison like hmac.compare_digest(), theoretically enabling timing side-channel attacks to guess the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN character by character.]

Security headers intentionally stripped — Weakened browser-side defenses, making XSS and content injection attacks more impactful. [verified: Same as finding 12: browser X-XSS-Protection disabled and Content-Security-Policy emptied, stripping defense-in-depth against XSS and content injection.]

Explicit disabling of X-XSS-Protection and Content-Security-Policy headers — Weakened browser XSS defenses and no CSP enforcement, increasing the exploitation surface for any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the application. [verified: Same as finding 12: X-XSS-Protection explicitly set to '0' and Content-Security-Policy set to empty string, disabling browser XSS filtering and CSP enforcement on responses.]

TLS certificate verification disabled — Man-in-the-middle attacks on outbound HTTPS connections, credential/token interception. [verified: Same as finding 11: TLS certificate verification explicitly disabled via ssl._create_unverified_context() for outbound HTTPS request, enabling MITM interception.]

Information disclosure — internal paths and configuration exposed in response — Attacker learns internal filesystem layout (private_exports directory location) and Django configuration module path, aiding further attacks. [verified: Same as finding 13: payroll_trace_panel_443 exposes DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and BASE_EXPORT_DIR in response, leaking internal filesystem paths and configuration.]

Information exposure — internal paths and settings leaked — Reconnaissance information that aids path traversal and other targeted attacks. [verified: Same as finding 13: payroll_trace_panel_443 exposes DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and BASE_EXPORT_DIR path in JSON response, leaking internal configuration details.]

Security header stripping in ops route — Disables browser XSS auditor and CSS injection protections, making it easier to exploit XSS or CSS injection vulnerabilities if the response content is reflected in a browser context. [verified: Same as finding 12: X-XSS-Protection set to '0' and Content-Security-Policy set to empty string, actively disabling browser security defenses on responses from this endpoint.]

Sensitive Data Exposure — Environment Variables and Filesystem Paths in Response — An attacker learns the internal filesystem layout (BASE_EXPORT_DIR path) and Django settings module location, aiding in path traversal attacks, targeted file reads, and reconnaissance for further exploitation. [verified: Same as finding 13: endpoint returns internal environment variable values and filesystem paths, aiding attackers in mapping the application's internal structure.]

Information exposure of internal paths and configuration in ops route — Reveals server filesystem layout and Django configuration module to attackers, aiding in path traversal, file write, and other targeted attacks against the deployment. [verified: Same as finding 13: endpoint returns DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and BASE_EXPORT_DIR in JSON response, leaking deployment internals that aid further attacks.]

Webhook Secret Exposed as Plaintext in Edit Form HTML — An attacker with access to the HR admin's browser can extract the webhook HMAC signing secret from the rendered edit form HTML, enabling forged webhook deliveries and potential downstream exploitation of systems consuming those webhooks. [verified: The WebhookForm secret field lacks widget=forms.PasswordInput, rendering the HMAC secret as plain <input type=text> in HTML source when an HR admin views the webhook_edit page (views.py:326-332); this enables visual interception via shoulder-surfing or unattended screens despite @hr_admin_required, though impact is limited by local-only mocked webhook delivery and the HR-admin authentication gate.]
